..
Issued at 1104 PM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

Upper level ridging was in control this evening, giving us 
mostly clear skies and keeping temperatures in the 70s across 
most of the area. At the surface, a cold front was pushing 
southeast into northeast NE, stretching from around Sioux City 
to Norfolk to Albion as of 11 PM. It's not expected to make much
more progress overnight, so north of that line, expect lows in 
the upper 50s and 60s, and south of that line, expect lows right
around 70.

The front will begin to slowly edge southward during the day on
Monday, pushing into far southeast NE and southwest IA by the 
evening. Areas that remain ahead of the front most of the day 
will see another hot day with highs in the lower 90s (likely 
breaking records), while areas behind will be in the 70s and 
80s. By the evening, guidance is in decent agreement that we'll 
see at least some precip development along the boundary as 
moisture transport strengthens. Model soundings continue to show
quite a bit of dry air to overcome, but also a little 
instability to work with, so think things will be spotty, but 
wouldn't rule out a few rumbles of thunder. Maintaining a 20% 
chance of showers and storms.

The boundary looks to remain in the NE/KS/IA/MO border area on 
Tuesday, though still quite a bit of spread in guidance on 
exactly where it sets up (could be over our area or could be to 
the south). The general idea is that storms will develop along 
the boundary in the afternoon/evening as a surface low develops 
over southeast CO and western KS and some shortwave energy 
coming from both a large scale trough over the Desert Southwest 
and from Hurricane Simon off the west coast of Mexico arrives in
the area. The advection of warm, moist air ahead of the 
boundary during the day will lead to a decently unstable airmass
with guidance suggesting 1000-2000 J/kg of SBCAPE. Shear will 
also be plenty strong to yield a strong to severe storm threat, 
though with largely boundary-parallel shear, storms could be a 
little messy. Finally, with at least some tropical influence, 
expect efficient rain production with precipitable water values 
around 1.75 inches, so can't rule out some flooding wherever the
primary rain band sets up. Again, the big question will be 
where the storms develop. Many CAMs (e.g. 12.00Z HRRR) keep 
things largely south of our area, though a few REFS members 
would suggest areas near and south of a Fairbury to Nebraska 
City to Red Oak line would have at least some severe weather 
threat (up to 15% chance).

Precip looks to expand north of the boundary later Tuesday 
evening as isentropic ascent picks up. We should see a break for
much of the area during the day Wednesday before more 
widespread chances arrive Wednesday evening and last into 
Thursday as the large scale trough to our west moves in. Still a
fair amount of spread on how exactly that system evolves, 
mainly impacting how long rain lingers into Thursday. Some 
guidance suggests the wave moves through very quickly or we get 
a strong punch of dry air and most of Thursday is dry. Other 
solutions linger a deformation band of rain across the area into
Thursday evening. For now, precip chances are in the 60-80% 
range through noon and drop to around 20-30% after.

We'll dry out after that as another trough drops southeast out 
of Canada and into the Great Lakes while cool high pressure 
builds in across the forecast area. Temperatures through the 
week steadily decrease, with widespread 60s to lower 70s 
Wednesday and Thursday followed by 50s and lower 60s Friday. The
coldest night will be Friday night, with lows dipping into the 
30s. Latest guidance is trending toward lower probabilities for 
a true freeze (20-30% chance of getting below 32 degrees) as the
trough out of Canada is tracking farther east, but some patchy 
frost may be possible that night.
